newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open a bit lower before jobless data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open a bit lower before jobless data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened slightly lower on Thursday in front of the government's weekly release on new jobless claims.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that new claims for state unemployment insurance totaled 337,000 in the latest week versus 342,000 a week earlier. The data are due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was off 2/32 to 101-10/32, yielding 6.40 percent in early trade.
Analysts said the market was likely to be range-bound on Thursday as players take a cautious view in front of Friday's November unemployment report.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that non-farm payrolls experienced "below-trend" growth of 179,000 jobs in November following an expansion of payrolls by 210,000 jobs in October.

A number near forecasts would keep the market in its current range. A number much below forecast, could send the 30-year bond yield to 6.25 pct, said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets.
Treasury prices fell on Wednesday as disappointment over the absence of a Federal Reserve coupon pass prompted selling.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 14/32 in late trade.

The only other economic data the market will get today is the governmemt's revised third-quarter productivity figures at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. Economists expect that number to be revised down to -0.1 percent from the preliminary figure of a 0.2 percent rise. Those data are not expected to sway the market.
The Treasury will sell $19.25 billion in 52-week bills, a bit of supply that dealers believe the market will readily absorb. The bidding deadline is 1300 EST/1800 GMT.
The question of whether the Fed will add permament reserves to the banking system has been in front of the market since before Thanksgiving and has come to haunt it.

"The question of whether the Fed buys coupons is a very important fact for the market because a lot of people are so long," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "A lot of people own securities because they got caught up in the momentum of the rally and that portion of the market hasn't gotten any gratification from the good news while they've been frustrated by the lack of a coupon pass."
Complicating matters is a rumor circulating that maybe the Fed has found other ways to manage reserves and maybe will not need to buy coupons at all.
"That's what everybody is talking about," said Stiles.

The discussion swirls in a market where durations are the highest they have been since the last rally ended, said Stiles. "You see very high bullish readings. Repo rates seem to be higher than they usually would be, suggesting that there's a lot of leveraged positions getting financed.
"There are a lot of reasons to believe people are fully committed here," he said.

"The most interesting thing about the yield structure is that there's no cushion for a strong fourth quarter and we won't know how good the fourth quarter is until a little bit into 1997," said Stiles.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.90 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were up one and two basis points, respectively, to 4.99 percent and 5.13 percent.
The two-year note was down 1/32 to 99-30, yielding 5.66 percent. Five-year notes were down 3/32 to 99-27/32, yielding 5.91 percent. Ten-year notes were down 6/32 to 102-23/32, yielding 6.13 percent.
